summary:
CosmoSphere is a website where you fly around the solar system and find the NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars. You pick a planet, drag a timeline from 1950 to 2026, and click any of 29 pieces of equipment to see what it was, when it launched and what happened to it. That includes Apollo 11’s Eagle, Surveyor 3 and the parachute Perseverance left on Mars.

There is also a story mode. A mascot called Pip takes you through all 29 objects in launch order, and every number Pip says comes from the data behind the markers.

We made it for casual space fans, who mostly hear about missions that are still running. The old landers and rovers are just as interesting, but their details sit in dense catalogs. We wanted people to see where each one is and care about what it did. We also researched 104 Moon and Mars landing and crash sites from NASA’s NSSDCA and LROC, and we label uncertain locations as approximate.
details:
What it does and how it works:
CosmoSphere is a website that works like a console. You pick a planet from a bar along the top, drag a timeline from 1950 to 2026, and click any of 29 pieces of NASA hardware (14 on the Moon, 14 on Mars, one in Earth orbit). Each one opens an inspector with its mission, year, agency and status, plus a wireframe preview. You can also search for a machine by name or type and the camera flies to it. In story mode, a mascot called Albert takes you through all 29 objects in launch order, and every number Albert says comes from the same data behind the markers.

Why it’s useful and what we want it to do:
Most kids only hear about missions that are still running. The old landers, rovers and crashed probes are interesting too, but their details sit in dense catalogs. We want students to see where each machine ended up and care about what it found.

Tools:
We built it with Three.js (r169), Vite and plain JavaScript modules, with no framework. Pip’s voice is made from synthesized sounds in the browser, not recordings. For accuracy we used NASA’s NSSDCA, LROC (the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera team at ASU), NASA mission pages, the Planetary Society and published papers.

What’s creative:
The hardware shows up as characters on a real map of the solar system, with a guide, a tour and a clock you can scrub. We also drew planets three times larger and orbits ten times wider than real so the markers stay clickable, while the order of the solar system stays correct.

What we considered:
Accuracy came first. We also compiled a research table of 104 Moon and Mars landing and crash sites, and where a location is uncertain, such as Luna 9, we labeled it approximate instead of guessing. We kept the whole thing in a browser so a classroom doesn’t need to install anything, and we credited every outside source.
